common_name: Itsaul White Dianthus (Heat-Tolerant Groundcover Pink with Fragrant White Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Itsaul White is a fast-spreading groundcover selection valued for its heat and humidity tolerance in southern gardens.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Itsaul White forms a fast-spreading, dense evergreen mat of fine silvery-blue foliage that fills in more quickly than many older garden pink cultivars, making it a popular choice for edging, slopes, and mass groundcover plantings. In late spring it produces an abundant flush of small, single to semi-double, clove-scented white flowers held just above the foliage. It holds up notably well to the summer heat and humidity of the southeastern United States, a trait that has made it a mainstay in southern nursery trade offerings, though like other dianthus it still demands sharp drainage to avoid crown rot. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to keep the mat tight and encourage fresh foliage growth.

common_name: First Love Dianthus (Color-Changing First-Year-Flowering Interspecific Sweet William)

planting.note: Direct sow or plant transplants in fall for spring bloom in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; First Love is an interspecific sweet william bred to flower the first year from an early seed start and to change color as blooms age.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. First Love is an interspecific Sweet William notable for its color-changing flower clusters: individual florets open nearly white and gradually deepen through shades of pink to a deeper rose as they age, so a single cluster displays several tones at once for a shifting, multicolor effect over the bloom season. Unlike heirloom biennial sweet williams that need a full season of vegetative growth before flowering, it blooms the first year from an early seed start, extending its usefulness as a bedding and cutting plant. Deadheading spent clusters encourages continued flowering from late spring into summer, and the compact, well-branched habit suits the front of a border as well as containers.

common_name: Little Jock Dianthus (Compact Double Cheddar Pink with Maroon Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; Little Jock is a compact cheddar pink selection with double, soft pink flowers marked with a dark maroon eye.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Little Jock forms a dense, tight cushion of fine, silvery-blue evergreen foliage only a few inches tall, well suited to rock gardens, wall crevices, and trough plantings. In late spring it bears double, soft pink flowers with a distinct dark maroon eye at the center and a strong clove fragrance, carried on short stems just above the foliage mound. Its very compact, slow-spreading habit makes it slower to fill in than larger cheddar pink cultivars, but keeps it neat and long-lived in a small-scale planting. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to maintain the tight cushion form.
